title: Great Lent
hookLine: Eastern Lent begins on Clean Monday with stricter fasting

lines: THE PRIEST BOWS TO THE PEOPLE.
cards: Sunday evening, in a Byzantine Catholic church. Vespers has just ended, and the priest steps down, bows to the people, and asks their forgiveness. Then the people line up and bow to each other, one by one.
Forgive me, a sinner. God forgives, the other answers. A teenager bows to her grandmother.

Two men who haven't spoken in months end up face to face in the line. The next morning there are no ashes, no Wednesday. Lent has simply begun, on a Monday, with a name that sounds like a fresh sheet of paper.

teach.b: Eastern Christians call it Great Lent, and its first day Clean Monday. The idea is in Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "Wash yourselves, be clean." Not a scrubbed kitchen, though some families do clean house.
A clean heart, after a night of forgiving and being forgiven.
Then the fast. Western Catholics today fast on a few set days of Lent and abstain from meat on its Fridays.
The traditional Byzantine fast asks more: through the whole season, meat and dairy are set aside, and on Clean Monday some people eat very little at all.
Eastern Catholic churches differ in how strictly they keep it now, and people are often given gentler rules for health or work. Eastern teachers say the point was never the menu.
It's freedom: a body that learns it can say no to a craving can learn to say yes to God.
In Byzantine churches, a short prayer attributed to Saint Ephrem the Syrian is said on weekdays of Lent with deep bows.
It asks God to take away laziness, discouragement, the lust for power and idle talk, and to give chastity, humility, patience and love, and the grace to see one's own faults and not judge a brother.
Last, Jesus's own instruction about fasting, which East and West both read: "But thou, when thou fastest anoint thy head, and wash thy face."

teach.h: ANOINT THY HEAD, AND WASH THY FACE.
teach.b: No show. Fasting done cleanly, from Clean Monday to the feast.

how: In the Byzantine Catholic churches, Great Lent begins on Clean Monday after Forgiveness Sunday vespers, where people ask one another's forgiveness; the traditional fast sets aside meat and dairy, and the Prayer of Saint Ephrem is said with prostrations on Lenten weekdays.

games.q: it's the Sunday evening before Lent. the priest has just bowed to the congregation and asked their forgiveness. what happens next?
o: the people bow to each other and ask forgiveness, one by one.
the priest hears confessions until midnight.
games.why: at Forgiveness Vespers, people bow to one another: forgive me, a sinner. God forgives. Lent begins the next morning, on Clean Monday.

practice: Think of your next meal, or tomorrow's, and picture it plainer: bread and soup, rice and beans, one dish instead of three, eaten slowly without the phone.
Then notice what that small freedom might make room for: an apology, a phone call, a moment of prayer, money to give away.
If you pray, offer the plain meal for someone who has too little; if you don't, let it be a small act of attention.

wordCard.voice: Great Lent. The Eastern season of fasting before Pascha, beginning on Clean Monday, after a Sunday of mutual forgiveness, with a longer and stricter fast. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: clean monday. Here, Lent begins with forgiveness, before the first fast. Go gently.
